content: The text provided is a dense compilation of references and summaries of studies related to the prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV. 1. A program in Uganda aimed at preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV was evaluated, with findings published in AIDS (London, England) in 2005. The study focused on mothers receiving short-course antiretroviral therapy (ART). 2. Mandala et al. utilized service data to assess pediatric HIV-free survival outcomes following PMTCT programs in rural Malawi. This study, published in BMC Public Health in 2012, included mothers who received single-dose nevirapine (NVP). 3. Minniear et al. examined outcomes in a cohort of women who discontinued maternal triple-antiretroviral regimens after labor. The study highlighted the challenges of ART discontinuation and its implications for PMTCT. 4. Studies included in this analysis were selected based on specific search criteria outlined in Appendix 1. Some studies were additional outputs of larger research projects, which produced further papers and reports not considered in this review. 5. Between 2003 and 2009 in Kenya, ART was initially used to prevent mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Findings were published in PLoS One in 2014. 6. Mwendo et al. evaluated the effectiveness of PMTCT programs in the Kilimanjaro region of northern Tanzania. The study, published in Tropical Medicine & International Health in 2014, reported that nearly 50% of losses occurred during the first PCR test, with only seven children completing 18 months of follow-up. 7. Nagot et al. compared lopinavir/ritonavir with lamivudine as peri-exposure prophylaxis to prevent HIV-1 transmission through breastfeeding. The PROMISE-PEP trial, published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2012, included mothers who were not eligible for ART. 8. Nlend and Ekani conducted a preliminary assessment of breastfeeding practices among HIV-1-infected mothers under the Djoungolo PMTCT program in Cameroon. The study, published in Journal of Tropical Pediatrics in 2010, focused on breastfeeding, mastitis, and transmission, with assessments conducted at 13 weeks postpartum. 9. Nyandiko et al. evaluated the outcomes of HIV-exposed children in western Kenya, focusing on the efficacy of PMTCT in resource-constrained settings. The study, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010, noted difficulties in extracting data on transmission and mortality for mothers on ART and breastfeeding. 10. Omer et al. conducted a 12-month follow-up of six-week extended-dose nevirapine randomized controlled trials. The study, published in AIDS (London, England) in 2011, highlighted the differential impact of extended-dose nevirapine on mother-to-child transmission and infant mortality based on maternal CD4 cell counts. 11. Palombi et al. described the Treatment Acceleration Program and the DREAM program's experience in PMTCT. The study, published in AIDS (London, England) in 2007, shared data from the DREAM study, which was also included in another selected study. 12. Read reviewed antiretroviral strategies for PMTCT in Clinics in Perinatology in 2010. The study noted that very few mothers were on ART. 13. Seth et al. reported on the outcomes of HIV-exposed infants at a regional pediatric HIV center in North India. The study, published in Indian Journal of Pediatrics in 2012, highlighted the limited number of mothers on ART and the lack of information on whether these mothers were breastfeeding. 14. Shah et al. assessed the cost-effectiveness of new WHO recommendations for PMTCT in resource-limited settings. The study, published in AIDS (London, England) in 2011, was based on adherence models in Nigeria. 15. Simpore et al. evaluated an effective PMTCT program at Saint Camille Medical Centre in Burkina Faso. The study, published in Journal of Medical Virology in 2007, included a very small number of breastfed children. 16. Stringer et al. measured population-level HIV-free survival among children under two years of age in four African countries. The study, published in PLoS Medicine in 2013, provided data on HIV-free survival for mothers on ART or dual antiretroviral therapy. 17. Taha et al. updated the efficacy results of the PEPFAR-Malawi trial, which investigated post-exposure prophylaxis for breastfeeding HIV-exposed infants with antiretroviral drugs up to 14 weeks of age. The study, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2011, compared outcomes among mothers not on ART and those on dual therapy. 18. Torpey et al. examined infant feeding options and other non-chemoprophylactic factors influencing mother-to-child HIV transmission in Zambia. The study, published in Journal of the International Association of Physicians in AIDS Care in 2012, lacked data on mothers on ART and breastfeeding simultaneously. 19. Torpey et al. also estimated mother-to-child transmission rates in a PMTCT program setting in Zambia. The study, published in Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2010, similarly lacked data on mothers on ART and breastfeeding together. 20. Van Lettow et al. reported on the uptake and outcomes of a PMTCT program in Zomba District, Malawi. The study, published in BMC Public Health, provided data on transmission and excluded deaths within 24 hours. 21. Alvarez-Uria et al. evaluated PMTCT outcomes in India across three hospitals, focusing on HAART, breastfeeding, and replacement feeding. The study provided data on transmission and mortality from the first week postpartum. 22. Thistle et al. assessed PMTCT outcomes in Zimbabwe, focusing on HAART and breastfeeding. The study calculated transmission and mortality rates between 14 and 36 weeks postpartum. 23. Homsy et al. evaluated PMTCT outcomes in Uganda, focusing on HAART and breastfeeding. The study calculated transmission and mortality rates from the first antenatal visit through 18 months postpartum. 24. Peltier et al. assessed PMTCT outcomes in Rwanda, focusing on HAART, breastfeeding, and replacement feeding. The study provided data on transmission and mortality from 48 hours postpartum. 25. Marazzi et al. evaluated PMTCT outcomes in Mozambique, focusing on HAART and breastfeeding. The study provided data on transmission and mortality at 15 weeks postpartum. 26. Kilewo et al. assessed PMTCT outcomes in Tanzania, focusing on HAART and breastfeeding. The study provided data on transmission and mortality at 34 weeks postpartum. 27. Tonwe-Gold et al. evaluated PMTCT outcomes in Côte d’Ivoire, focusing on HAART, short-course ART, and single-dose nevirapine. The study provided data on transmission and mortality at 24 weeks postpartum. 28. Sagay et al. assessed PMTCT outcomes in Nigeria, focusing on HAART and breastfeeding. The study provided data on transmission and mortality over a one-year period. 29. Ngoma et al. evaluated PMTCT outcomes in Zambia, focusing on HAART and breastfeeding. The study provided data on transmission and mortality over a one-year period. 30. The Newcastle-Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale was modified for this study to evaluate the quality of included studies. The scale assessed selection, comparability, and outcome measures, with specific criteria for adherence to ART, breastfeeding practices, and HIV-free survival outcomes.
